Categories.value: Rain in art|Will Vawter|Author died more than 70 years ago public domain images|Bobbs-Merrill Company|1899 illustrations|PD US expired|CC-PD-Mark|PD-old missing SDC copyright status|PD-US missing SDC copyright status|Running people in art|Riley Child-Rhymes

ImageDescription.value:
An illustration for James Whitcomb Riley's poem "A Sudden Shower", appearing in the 1899 edition of Riley Child-Rhymes.

It shows a street scene with a group of children covering their heads as they run in the sudden rainfall.

This was one of illustrator Will Vawter's "Hoosier Pictures", depicting nostalgic, rural Indiana scenes, with images including barefooted children, farm life, and rural landscapes.

The poem this image accompanies, "A Sudden Shower", begins,

"Barefooted boys scud up the street,
Or skurry under sheltering sheds;
And schoolgirl faces, pale and sweet,
Gleam from the shawls about their heads."

135171799.title: File:Rain clouds finally approach Greenwich Park.jpg

ObjectName.value: Rain clouds finally approach Greenwich Park

Categories.value: Greenwich Park|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation (51° N, 1° W)|The Grand Ascent, Greenwich Park

ImageDescription.value:
Rain clouds finally approach Greenwich Park, its ground still savaged by weeks of extreme heat and drought.

Greenwich Park is just a short bus ride from where I live in London. It was not just the bleached grass that was shocking - many of the trees were already losing their leaves and younger trees looked seriously stressed. London and much of Europe have seen many weeks of extreme heat and drought.

The mainstream media reprimands individuals for wasting water, justifiably exhorting us to limit our showers, but all the while ignoring the highly profitable water companies which fail to invest in infrastructure, reservoirs or leakage prevention. The media also overlooks the devastating impact of large scale agribusiness, particularly livestock farming, which places an increasingly unsustainable demand on the planet's scarce water resources, as well as further inflating emissions and driving deforestation.

Meanwhile, corporate greed is accelerating the consumption of fossil fuels and water and turbocharging climate change. We need rain. We need more regulation. More action. We need to get to net zero asap and water management should not be in private hands. Water companies are siphoning off enormous profits from a vital public utility and failing to invest anything like what is needed.

The head of Thames Water (the same company which dumped raw sewage into rivers over 5000 times in 2021) is set to pocket £3 million as a 'golden hello' for signing on as CEO ,while in total the UK's water companies have handed an average of around £2 billion every year to their shareholders in dividends since they were privatised. If they were nationalised, those profits could instead have been invested to upgrade the infrastructure and mitigate the impact of climate change and have even provided extra funds to promote sustainable alternative energy sources.

www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/apr/20/thames-water-...

www.theguardian.com/environment/2020/jul/01/england-priva...

As Caroline Lucas writes in the Guardian (12.08.22) - ' (Drought) is a consequence of years of inaction on the climate emergency. This is producing a perfect storm of energy insecurity, food supply chaos and extreme weather that is wreaking havoc on society.'

www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2022/aug/12/drought-uk-...

ObjectName.value: Rainbow viewed from the Beachcomber Cafe, Praa Sands - geograph.org.uk - 526173

Categories.value: Rain showers|Taken with Olympus SP-500UZ|Images from Geograph Britain and Ireland|Rainbows in the United Kingdom|Information field template with formatting|Images by Jim Champion|United Kingdom photographs taken on 2007-08-12|Rain in August 2007|Praa Sands beach

ImageDescription.value: Rainbow viewed from the Beachcomber Cafe, Praa Sands As a rain shower faded and the sunlight emerged through a gap in the clouds this very vivid rainbow appeared across the bay. This view is from the terrace of the Beachcomber Cafe. In physics parlance the rainbow is a virtual image, existing only in the sense that your optical system perceives a coloured arc "out there" (or in this case my camera's optical system). There was a good reflected bow off the sea, and the secondary bow (with the spectrum reversed) is visible to the right. We had just ordered some food as we sheltered from the rain, but as the rainbow appeared everyone (staff included) headed out of the cafe to watch and photograph this picturesque scene.

ImageDescription.value:
xi pages, 280 : 18 cm
Mary Hunter Austin (1868-1934) moved with her family from Illinois to the desert on the edge of the San Joaquin Valley in 1888. In the next fifteen years she moved from one desert community to another, working on her sketches of desert and Indian life. Spending the last years of her life in Santa Fe, Austin remained a lifelong defender of Native Americans and was recoginzed as an expert in Native American poetry. The land of little rain (1903), Austin's first book, focuses on the arid and semi-arid regions of California between the High Sierras south of Yosemite: the Ceriso, Death Valley, the Mojave Desert; and towns such as Jimville, Kearsarge, and Las Uvas. She writes of the region's climate, plants, and animals and of its people: the Ute, Paiute, Mojave, and Shoshone tribes; European-American gold prospectors and borax miners; and descendants of Hispanic settlers
